I have a serious Concern regarding USD/INR exchange rate and transparency of charges I am disappointed with the way USD deposits are being processed through INDmoney/Federal Bank. I recently tried to deposit ₹50,000 into my US wallet, and the app showed an exchange rate of ₹96.25/USD, while the prevailing USD/INR rate at the time was around ₹94.26/USD. This represents a difference of approximately ₹1.99 per USD, or 2.1%, which is significant for a currency conversion. For a ₹50,000 transaction, this exchange-rate difference alone can materially reduce the USD amount received. The app also displayed ₹74.89 GST and ₹8,321 indicative TCS. I understand that TCS is refundable and therefore should not necessarily be considered a permanent cost. However, the exchange-rate spread is a separate issue and needs much greater transparency. My concern is not simply about paying a fee — it is about fair and transparent valuation of the money being converted. If Federal Bank/INDmoney is applying a currency-conversion markup, customers should clearly be shown the reference USD/INR rate, the markup/spread being applied, and the exact amount being charged because of that spread. The statement “You’re saving ₹1,796 on transfer charges and forex rates” also creates the impression that the conversion is highly competitive, while the displayed exchange rate appears materially higher than the prevailing market rate. I request INDmoney to clearly disclose how this exchange rate is determined and what portion of the difference represents the bank’s forex spread. Customers should be able to see a transparent calculation before approving the transaction. Please improve the transparency of USD/INR conversion rates and ensure customers receive a fair and properly evaluated exchange rate

Essential Risk Management Feature Missing in INDmoney. INDmoney is a solid platform overall, but there’s one critical feature missing that can seriously impact traders, especially those who care about proper risk management. Once a trade is placed, users should be able to set both Stop Loss (SL) and Take Profit (TP) orders at the same time. Right now, the limitation forces traders to manage positions manually or place orders separately, which increases risk and leaves room for error in fast moving markets. This is not just a nice feature. It is essential. For traders, even a small delay or missed execution can make a big difference in outcomes. Having both SL and TP in place from the start ensures discipline, protects capital, and removes emotional decision making during volatility. Another important point is that many traders prefer working with absolute numbers rather than percentages. Not everyone manages trades in percentages. Clear, number based inputs for SL and TP would make the platform more practical and user friendly for real trading scenarios. A small upgrade like this could significantly improve the trading experience on INDmoney. It is about giving traders the control they need to manage risk properly

Now it only shows overall portfolio 1D change, which reduces visibility into individual fund performance. • Peer comparison details are gone. Previously, we could easily check where a mutual fund ranked within its category and compare it against category averages. That feature was extremely useful for analysis. • Fund exploration and filtering also feels limited now. Earlier it was easier to browse and filter funds based on our own requirements. The new UI may look cleaner, but a lot of practical investor-focused insights from the old version are missing. Would really appreciate if these features could be brought back. Otherwise, users looking for detailed analysis and fund comparison may eventually prefer alternatives like INDmoney or similar platforms

Transactions Tracking and Payments Integration- Serious Issue. Kuvera is definitely has lots of gaps. After using Kuvera as direct MF platform for past 1 year (almost), I would like to highlight some serious issues. List below. 1) UPI integration is definitely not seamless. You are lucky, if there is a success. 30% it fails and you need to wait for reflection or initiate payment again. Kuvera doesn’t have proper tracking of UPI failures - instead you need to share all proofs for their support team to validate and complete the transactions. Leads to serious frustration- when your funds are in dark and status unknown. 2) When markets are highly volatile - avoid using Kuvera for MF investments. Even if you have success on the transaction, there is a possibility that your NAV is not of same day. Kuvera generally puts it back in BSEStar platform - which may be right, but for me I expected their platform to be resilient. Currently, stability is a serious issue. You lose if NaV is low for that day and Kuvera considers next days NaV. Also, to prove that your side of transactions are done perfectly - we need to share everything. In the digital world, I wouldn’t expect customer to keep on sharing proofs to Kuvera team to prove that transactions are correctly submitted. 3) Support team has some gap in understanding queries. Many a times, multiple emails has to be triggered to explain the scenario and finally you get a response - which is completely out of context. 4) I still struggle for transaction units which are lost through Kuvera - still don’t have a trace of what happened and kept proving that it’s missing. Analysis and response from support is definitely a concern. 5) Kuvera is still not in a matured state and would expect them to standardise their operations, support, stability, resilience and finally transactions tracking seamlessly. - all above are my experience. Maybe a different user might have better experience, but 1 year on platform - these concerns are definitely to be addressed by Kuvera

text: Interesting video Akshat, but I think this analysis oversimplifies things a bit. SIP isn’t a trap — it’s a long-term wealth compounding tool used by some of the smartest minds in finance. If SIPs were really as ineffective as you suggest, do you think top fund houses like HDFC, Mirae, or even global legends like Warren Buffett would advocate for disciplined compounding and market participation? Also, inflation adjustment doesn’t mean you “lose” the value — it just reflects purchasing power. In real terms, ₹10K SIP for 30 years can still give 10x growth on purchasing power if you stay consistent. And one small thought — you often mention your consulting experience at BCG, which is great, but as someone from the investment banking world and with friends at BCG, I can tell you real financial depth comes from decades in the markets, not a few months or a short stint. Theory and real-world compounding are two very different things. Still appreciate the awareness angle — just think the headline figure of ₹38L is a bit exaggerated for effect.

text: From preplexity fact check like he said: "The video mixes some valid points (inflation, costs, volatility) with several exaggerations and selective assumptions. Overall, SIPs are not “useless”, but the returns and risks are more nuanced than shown. Core numerical claimsA 10,000/month SIP for 30 years at 12% CAGR growing to about 3 crore in nominal terms is mathematically reasonable; standard SIP calculators give a similar ballpark.�Industry “standard” equity SIP returns of roughly 12–15% over long periods (10–15 years) are broadly consistent with historical data for diversified Indian equity funds, though they vary a lot by fund and period.�� Long‑term Indian CPI inflation has averaged around 6–7% since the 1960s, so using 6% as an illustrative long‑run number is not unreasonable, although recent years have often been lower (3–6%).��� Where the video stretches things is in:Treating one inflation number (6–9%) as if it will surely persist for 30 years, which is unknowable and historically volatile.�� Presenting a single “real” outcome (36 lakh invested becomes only 45–75 lakh in today’s money) as a near‑certain reality, when this depends heavily on chosen assumptions for return, costs, taxes, and inflation. None of those are fixed for 30 years.��� Inflation, tax and costsLong‑term inflation: World Bank and other series show India’s inflation has averaged about 7% since 1960, but has been closer to 4–6% in the past decade; there is no basis to state confidently that it “will be high” or that India is “about to be hit really badly” over the next 5–7 years—this is a macro view, not fact.��� LTCG on equity funds: Equity LTCG in India was indeed 0% before 2018 and later increased; current rates around 12.5% for certain categories are directionally correct, but future changes (like “they might make it 15%”) are speculation, not fact.� Expense ratios: Active equity mutual funds do cost more than passive index funds like Nifty 50, and a 1% annual cost difference compounded over decades can easily eat 25–35% of final corpus, so the “33% hit” is broadly in the right range.�� So: the directions (inflation erodes, tax and costs matter) are right; the level of certainty and alarm is not.SIPs “won’t make you rich”Historically, long‑term SIPs in well‑chosen equity funds have produced double‑digit returns for many investors; several diversified funds show 15–20 year CAGRs in the low‑ to mid‑teens.���� Whether that makes someone “rich” depends on contribution size and personal definition of wealth, not just on return math. Calling SIPs “won’t make you rich” is a rhetorical opinion, not an objective fact.A more accurate framing: SIPs are a tool for disciplined investing that can build substantial real wealth over decades, but they are not a magic shortcut and are very sensitive to:Asset chosen (good diversified equity vs expensive or poor funds)Return achieved (which is uncertain)Inflation pathTaxes and expensesClaims about NASDAQ and “superior markets”Long‑term data shows the Nasdaq Composite has indeed delivered strong returns; 10‑year annualised returns in USD have often been in the mid‑teens in the recent decade, so 16–17% is plausible for some rolling periods, but not a stable “guaranteed” long‑run rate.��� US tech / mega‑cap (“Magnificent 7”) stocks have outperformed the broader S&P 500 dramatically in recent years, but this outperformance has also been cyclical and concentrated in a few names.�� The leap from “has outperformed in the recent past” to “therefore you should move SIPs to US tech; NASDAQ will keep compounding 16–17% for 30 years” is an investment viewpoint, not a fact. Long‑term future equity returns in any market are uncertain.Bitcoin and “fixed‑supply assets”Bitcoin’s protocol‑level hard cap of 21 million coins is factually correct, and it is one of the few major financial assets with a clear coded maximum supply.� Statements like “Bitcoin is a million‑dollar bet or zero” and implying 5% allocation might turn half your portfolio are highly speculative scenarios, not evidence‑based forecasts. Crypto has gone through repeated large drawdowns historically; treating it as “very little risk” is misleading.� So: the description of supply is factual; the risk‑return framing is aggressive opinion.Macro statements about India, US and inflation“US exports inflation to India/emerging markets” is a loose description for how global monetary policy and dollar strength can transmit inflationary pressure, but it is not a directly measurable fact in the simple way presented; the actual transmission mechanism is complex and debated in research.� The assertion that “inflation is about to hit India really badly over the next 5–7 years” is a prediction that is not supported by any consensus forecast; current official targets and projections aim to keep CPI around 4% with a tolerance band.��� These are macro opinions, not established facts.Bottom line for youThe math demonstrations (compounding, impact of 1–3% change in return, costs, taxes, and inflation) are directionally sound and worth understanding. The conclusions (“SIPs will not make you rich”, “36 lakh will only become 45–75 lakh in real terms”, “US tech / Bitcoin are the clear solution”, “India will be hit badly by inflation”) are interpretations and predictions, not objective facts.Historical data suggests:Long‑term equity SIPs in low‑cost, diversified funds have generally beaten inflation meaningfully in India, though with high volatility.���� Future returns and inflation are uncertain; overreliance on any one market (India, US tech, or Bitcoin) is risky. Diversification and cost control are strongly supported by evidence.���"

Yet, I have not stopped investing. I continue every SIP without interruption. After receiving my salary, I also contribute regularly to my PPF and NPS. I am determined to secure my family’s future, even while dealing with immense challenges in the present. Yes, I am struggling. But I am also brave, disciplined, and intelligent enough to keep moving forward.

text: Respected Vijay Mantri Sir, While I hold your deep market expertise and financial wisdom in high regard, I strongly believe that traditional equity SIPs will fail to deliver meaningful real wealth going forward. Year 2008 was once in lifetime opportunity, it does not comes again and again. text: The four-parameter framework is solid: long-term rolling returns, fund nature (concentration level), reason for correction (sector allocation changes), and manager changes. Most people only look at the price drop and panic. That's how you lock in losses at 98 NAV right before it rebounds to 108. The concentrated vs. diversified point is critical. Motilal Oswal midcap with 27 stocks is high risk/high reward. HDFC with 77 stocks is basically an index fund with higher fees. Neither is "wrong" but you need to know which you own and why. The SIP data is the real gem. Investor A (never stopped) beat Investor B (paused during 15%+ drops) by 15% over the same period. Trying to time your SIPs is just market timing with extra steps. It doesn't work. And the defense sector example PE of 56 vs. 5-year average of 43 — is a reminder that "good theme" and "good price" are two different things. Wars don't care about valuations. Your portfolio should. Not advice. Just appreciating a framework that replaces fear with process.
